_metrics_basis: Owner-signed 2026-08-06 (O-3 discharged). FOUR BASES ARE NOW IN USE, and each entry declares its own in metrics_basis. (1) CI-MEASURED — delivery-engine, analystkit and opskit: their CI publishes a stats.json counted from the JUnit report of the run that executed the tests, and the site renders that count with the commit it was measured at and the timestamp of that measurement. The timestamp means WHEN THE MEASUREMENT LAST CHANGED, not when CI last ran: each repo commits its stats.json only when the count or the release anchor differs, so a run that measures the same number leaves the file alone (owner's ruling 2026-08-10). This is defect D-02's recorded upgrade path (DECISIONS 3.1.3a), landed 2026-08-10. The label is 'tests', not 'unit tests': the measurement counts what pytest executed and does not establish that every one is a unit test. The resume-stated baseline each replaced is retained in verified_metrics in this file and is NOT rewritten — only the rendered figure changed. (2) OWNER-MEASURED — TS-Sentry: figures from a local run, 2026-08-06, corroborated by the repo's pinned CI and coverage badges. Unchanged by the D-02 upgrade. (3) RESUME-STATED BASELINES — delivery-engine-fde, whose metrics are qualitative rather than counts and which publishes no stats.json. (4) REPO-STATED - Switchyard: the count is the source repository's own published figure (README, v1.0.0), with its stated definition of passed plus skipped; adopted by owner's ruling 2026-08-22. The repo publishes no stats.json yet, so its CI-MEASURED upgrade via the D-02 path is a named follow-up in that repo, not a claim made here. Every entry still renders a version anchor and an evidence link, so no figure travels without its source.

projects.name: Switchyard
projects.problem: A system that has never failed in front of you is a system you do not understand.
projects.method: A governed AI platform: a model gateway, a job queue, and an observability stack, running on local Kubernetes. It routes requests across local models by policy, falls back when one is unhealthy, meters and bills every caller, runs long jobs through a queue that survives a dead worker, traces and alerts on all of it, deploys itself from its own repository through Argo CD, and has been broken on purpose three times to find out what it actually does. The platform was broken on purpose three times, a worker killed mid-job, Redis killed, and an Ollama backend killed, to find out what it actually does rather than what its design says. Each drill has a root-cause analysis on the Google SRE postmortem fields, the recovery steps that were actually used are written up in a runbook, and the machine's measured ceilings are in a capacity note. Every gate proves it can fail: each gate carries a negative control that must refuse and a positive control that must accept, with a distinct reason per failure mode.
